lab_title: Unraveling Retrograde Motion: Earth, Mars, and the Heliocentric Shift
top_level_objectives: Identify and describe the visual appearance of apparent retrograde motion from Earth.
Explain how the relative orbital speeds of Earth and Mars create the illusion of retrograde motion.
Correlate the planet's distance from the Sun with the magnitude of its retrograde loop.
Evaluate why the heliocentric model provides a simpler, more elegant explanation for planetary motion than the geocentric model.

scenes.brief_purpose: Observe the phenomenon of retrograde motion from the perspective of an Earth-based observer.
key_visuals: A simulated night sky with constellations.
A glowing marker showing Mars's position over several weeks.
student_actions: Step through a timeline to watch Mars move eastward across the sky.
Observe the moment Mars halts, reverses into a loop, and resumes eastward motion.

scenes.brief_purpose: Visualize the solar system from a top-down, heliocentric perspective.
key_visuals: A 3D model of the inner solar system (Sun, Earth, Mars).
Orbital paths showing Earth moving faster than Mars.
student_actions: Use a slider to progress through the orbital dance of Earth and Mars.
Identify the specific moment Earth 'catches up' to Mars.

scenes.brief_purpose: Synthesize the two viewpoints to explain the loop.
key_visuals: Split-screen view showing the Earthbound sky and the top-down orbital model simultaneously.
Dashed lines tracing the line-of-sight from Earth to Mars against the background stars.
student_actions: Synchronize the two views to realize that the 'loop' occurs exactly when Earth passes Mars.
Manipulate the viewpoint to see how the line-of-sight 'appears' to move backward.

scenes.brief_purpose: Demonstrate how the distance of the planet affects the appearance of the retrograde loop.
key_visuals: Models of Jupiter and Saturn added to the solar system view.
Comparisons of the path 'traced' by each planet in the night sky.
student_actions: Select different planets (Mars, Jupiter, Saturn) to observe their unique retrograde loops.
Compare the loop size and duration for each planet based on its distance from the Sun.

scenes.brief_purpose: Challenge the geocentric model by attempting to explain retrograde motion without the Sun at the center.
key_visuals: A geocentric model with fixed Earth and complex epicycle paths.
student_actions: Attempt to manually trace Mars's movement using the complex epicycle model.
Compare the simplicity of the heliocentric explanation versus the complexity of the geocentric one.
